title: Count Fertile Pyramids in a Land
statement:
`grid` is an `m x n` matrix where `1` marks a fertile cell and `0` a barren one; every cell beyond the edges of the matrix is barren. Count two kinds of plots, where each plot is fixed by its apex cell `(r, c)` and its height `h` (the number of rows it spans):

- A **pyramid** has its apex on top. It holds every cell `(i, j)` with `r <= i <= r + h - 1` and `c - (i - r) <= j <= c + (i - r)`, so each row below the apex is one cell wider on both sides.
- An **inverse pyramid** has its apex at the bottom. It holds every cell `(i, j)` with `r - h + 1 <= i <= r` and `c - (r - i) <= j <= c + (r - i)`, so each row above the apex is one cell wider on both sides.

A plot is valid only when all of its cells are fertile and it contains more than one cell (that is, `h >= 2`). Return the number of valid pyramids plus the number of valid inverse pyramids.
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every apex and every height, then checking each cell, is far too slow on a large grid. Notice instead that a pyramid of height `h` with apex `(r, c)` is exactly a fertile apex sitting on top of three pyramids of height `h - 1`, with apexes at `(r + 1, c - 1)`, `(r + 1, c)` and `(r + 1, c + 1)`: the two side ones cover the wide rows, and the middle one fills the single gap they leave just under the apex. So the tallest pyramid at a cell is one more than the smallest of the three below it. A cell whose tallest pyramid has height `H` is the apex of `H - 1` valid pyramids (heights `2` to `H`). Inverse pyramids are the same idea read from the top.

## Approach

1. Make two tables, `down` for pyramids and `up` for inverse pyramids, filled with `0` (a barren cell supports no plot).
2. Walk the rows from the bottom up. A fertile cell on the last row or on a side column can only be a single cell, height `1`. Any other fertile cell gets `1 + min` of the three `down` values in the row below.
3. Add `down[r][c] - 1` to `total` for every fertile cell.
4. Walk the rows from the top down and do the same for `up`, looking at the row above.
5. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`grid = [[0,1,1,0],[1,1,1,1]]`. Bottom-up: row 1 is the last row, so `down[1] = [1,1,1,1]`. In row 0, cell `(0,1)` gets `1 + min(1,1,1) = 2` and so does `(0,2)`, adding `1 + 1`. Top-down: row 0 is the first row, `up[0] = [0,1,1,0]`. In row 1, `(1,1)` gets `1 + min(0,1,1) = 1` and `(1,2)` gets `1 + min(1,1,0) = 1`, adding nothing. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m · n): each cell is visited once per pass with constant work.
- Space: O(m · n) for the two tables (one rolling row each would also do).

## Pitfalls

- Taking only the two side cells below misses the gap right under the apex; the middle cell must be in the `min` too.
- A tallest height `H` contributes `H - 1` plots, not `H`: single cells do not count.
- Edge columns and the first or last row can never be the apex of a plot of height 2 or more in that direction.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `m`, `n` | number of rows and columns |
| `down[r][c]` | tallest all-fertile pyramid with apex `(r, c)` |
| `up[r][c]` | tallest all-fertile inverse pyramid with apex `(r, c)` |
| `total` | plots counted so far |
| `r`, `c` | current row and column |

narration.4: down[r][c] will hold the height of the tallest pyramid whose apex is (r, c).
narration.5: up[r][c] does the same for inverse pyramids, whose apex is at the bottom.
narration.8: Pyramids grow downward, so fill down from the last row upward.
narration.10: A barren cell cannot be part of any plot; its height stays 0.
narration.13: On the last row or a side column there is no room to widen, so only the single cell fits.
narration.16: Otherwise the pyramid can be one taller than the smallest of the three pyramids just below it.
narration.18: A tallest height of H gives H - 1 plots of height at least 2 with this apex.
narration.22: Inverse pyramids grow upward, so fill up from the first row downward.
narration.27: On the first row or a side column only the single cell fits.
narration.30: One taller than the smallest of the three inverse pyramids just above.
narration.32: Count the inverse pyramids that have this cell as their bottom apex.
narration.35: total now holds every pyramid and every inverse pyramid.
